Beyond this core operational difference, vector databases provide production-ready features such as standard data management capabilities (inserting, deleting, updating) and metadata storage, which make them more operationally robust than standalone vector indices or traditional databases when dealing with complex vector data.

## Summary
The primary difference is that RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document to predict each target token, whereas RAG-Token marginalizes over the top retrieved documents for each individual token generation step.

## Key Points
*   RAG-Sequence employs a single document to predict every token in the target sequence.
*   RAG-Token generates a distribution for the next output token for each of the top K retrieved documents before marginalizing them.
*   For sequence classification tasks where the target sequence length is one, RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent.
*   Retrieving more documents at test time monotonically improves Open-domain QA results for RAG-Sequence, while performance for RAG-Token peaks at 10 retrieved documents.

## Elaboration
The core distinction lies in how the models handle the latent retrieved documents during generation. In RAG-Sequence, the model commits to using the same document to predict each target token throughout the sequence. In contrast, RAG-Token operates by having the generator produce a distribution for the next output token for each document in the top-K set, then marginalizes over these distributions before repeating the process for the subsequent token. This architectural difference leads to varied performance characteristics; for instance, increasing the number of retrieved documents consistently boosts RAG-Sequence performance in open-domain QA, whereas RAG-Token performance peaks with 10 documents. Additionally, the two models yield identical results for classification tasks where the output is a single token.
